title: 66 Lawmakers Urge Trump Administration to Halt Afghan Deportation Flights
excerpt: A bicameral letter led by Rep. Scott Peters asks Secretaries Rubio and Mullin to cancel flights that would send at least 150 Afghans from Louisiana to Pakistan — with Afghanistan, an ICE officer's court declaration says, the intended final destination.
body:
• Sixty-six members of Congress, led by Rep. Scott Peters, wrote to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Monday demanding the immediate cancellation of deportation flights carrying Afghans and Iranians.
  • The letter cites advocacy-group reports that at least 150 Afghans could be flown from detention in Louisiana to Pakistan from Tuesday, with relatives of Afghans who helped US troops possibly among them. An ICE officer's sworn court declaration, reported by CBS News, says the intended final destination is Afghanistan.
  • DHS declined to address the planned flights, citing operational security, but defended its third-country removal practices, saying deportees receive notice and assurances before removal.
  • For Afghan readers: the letter does not change anyone's status. Afghan Temporary Protected Status was terminated effective July 14, 2025; check your own position on the USCIS Afghanistan TPS page and with an immigration attorney.

A group of 66 lawmakers in the United States has written to the administration of President Donald Trump asking it to halt a planned mass deportation of Afghans, including some who worked alongside coalition forces in Afghanistan before the military withdrawal in 2021, Al Jazeera reported. Rep. Scott Peters of California led 65 bicameral members of Congress on the letter, sent Monday to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin, demanding the immediate cancellation of any deportation flights carrying Afghans and Iranians, whether sent directly or through another country, according to Peters' House office.

Who is affected

In Monday's letter, the lawmakers cited advocacy group reports that at least 150 Afghans were scheduled to be deported from Tuesday — flown from detention facilities in Louisiana to Pakistan, Al Jazeera reported. Human Rights First said it has confirmed that a flight carrying some of the Afghans from Alexandria, Louisiana, to Pakistan is scheduled for Tuesday. CBS News reported that a US immigration enforcement official confirmed in a sworn court declaration that a planned deportation flight originally scheduled for Tuesday, November 3, would land in Pakistan before an Afghan national would be transported onward to Afghanistan by land. "The plane's final destination would be Pakistan with further transport onward to Afghanistan," ICE supervisory detention and deportation officer Sergio Aguilar wrote in the October 30 declaration, adding that "the alien's intended removal destination was Afghanistan, as reflected in his removal order." A US official told CBS News the administration had made plans to deport nearly 200 Afghan nationals through Pakistan, while cautioning that the plans were still in flux. The lawmakers also expressed concern that relatives of Afghans who helped American troops could be among those on board, and raised alarm over reports of a separate mass deportation flight of Iranians.

"Sending dozens of people back to one of the most dangerous countries on earth, and where they are likely to be targeted for their or their family's suspected support of the US government or criticism of the Taliban, is a death sentence."

— The lawmakers' letter to Rubio and Mullin, via Al Jazeera

Why lawmakers say the flights break a promise

The members emphasized that the State Department lists Afghanistan as a Level 4 "Do Not Travel" country, and that for those who aided US forces, "their assistance to U.S. troops puts a target on these individuals and their families to this day." "Our nation made a promise to stand by Afghans who risked their lives and their families' safety to stand by U.S. service members," the members wrote, adding that deporting them "is a violation of that promise and our moral obligations to the Afghan community who stood alongside our troops." The members also stressed that routing a flight through a third country does not change US obligations, and urged the administration to warn Pakistan that the US will not accept its participation in sending deportees onward to the Taliban. The Associated Press reported that DHS officials had said in court filings that they eventually planned on returning some of the Afghans to their home country. The US does not have diplomatic relations with Afghanistan, which has been governed by the Taliban since US troops withdrew in August 2021.

The administration's position

The Department of Homeland Security declined to address the planned removal flights, citing operational security concerns, in a statement to CBS News, but defended its broader third-country removal practices. "Illegal aliens being sent to a third country receive notice and assurances prior to their removal," a DHS spokesperson said, adding that ICE receives diplomatic assurances from destination countries that deportees will be safe. The department did not specify whether Pakistan had provided such assurances for this operation. DHS referred questions about third-country agreements to the State Department; when Rubio was pressed about the planned Afghan deportations at an October 31 news conference, he directed the question back to DHS, CBS News reported. The deportations come after the administration terminated Temporary Protected Status for Afghanistan effective July 14, 2025 — in the termination notice, then-Secretary Kristi Noem found that Afghanistan no longer met the statute's conditions, citing "notable improvements in the security and economic situation." The USCIS page for Afghan TPS records the designation's end and the employment-authorization documents that ran through that date.

What happens next

The members requested an immediate response from Rubio and Mullin. Whether the Tuesday flight proceeds is now the immediate question: one Afghan man, identified in CBS News reporting by the surname Sadat, has already been removed from the flight list and released from ICE custody after a judge ruled his continued detention violated his due process rights, according to his attorney. For Afghans in the United States watching this unfold, the letter itself changes nothing legally — anyone with a removal order or a pending case should speak to an immigration attorney about their own position rather than rely on the outcome of a congressional appeal.
